stem: Mass of an atom of oxygen in gram is \(26.56896 \times 10^{-24}\) g. What is the atomic mass of oxygen in u ?
solution:
Mass of an atom of oxygen in gram is \(26.56896 \times 10^{-24}\) g, and

\(1.66056 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g} = 1\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(\therefore\ 26.56896 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g} = ?\)

\(= \dfrac{26.56896 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g}}{1.66056 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g/u}} = 16.0\ \mathrm{u}\)

Similarly mass of an atom of hydrogen \(= 1.0080\ \mathrm{u}\)
_note: p-06 left column, printed p.7. Carries its own `Solution :` label.

stem:
Calculate the average atomic mass of neon using the following data :

| Isotope | Atomic mass | Natural Abundance |
|---|---|---|
| \(^{20}\mathrm{Ne}\) | 19.9924 u | 90.92% |
| \(^{21}\mathrm{Ne}\) | 20.9940 u | 0.26 % |
| \(^{22}\mathrm{Ne}\) | 21.9914 u | 8.82 % |
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book prints the final value as 20.1707 u, but the expression printed immediately above it evaluates to 20.1713 u — \((19.9924 \times 90.92) + (20.9940 \times 0.26) + (21.9914 \times 8.82) = 2017.1316\), and dividing by 100 gives 20.17132. The abundances sum to exactly 100 %, and no alternative reading of the three printed isotopic masses or abundances produces 20.1707, so this is an arithmetic slip in the last two digits rather than a different data set. The working is correct and is preserved as printed; the method and the answer to four significant figures (20.17 u) are unaffected.]

Average atomic mass of Neon (Ne)

\(= \dfrac{\text{Atomic mass of } ^{20}\mathrm{Ne} \times \% \ +\ \text{Atomic mass of } ^{21}\mathrm{Ne} \times \% \ +\ \text{Atomic mass of } ^{22}\mathrm{Ne} \times \%}{100}\)

\(= \dfrac{(19.9924\,\mathrm{u})(90.92) + (20.9940\,\mathrm{u})(0.26) + (21.9914\,\mathrm{u})(8.82)}{100} = 20.1707\ \mathrm{u}\)
_note: p-07, spans the full page width across both columns. Stem carries the book's 3-row isotope table.

stem: Find the mass of 1 molecule of oxygen \((\mathrm{O_2})\) in amu (u) and in grams.
solution:
Molecular mass of \(\mathrm{O_2} = 2 \times 16\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(\therefore\) mass of 1 molecule \(= 32\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(\therefore\) mass of 1 molecule of \(\mathrm{O_2}\)

\(= 32.0 \times 1.66056 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g}\)

\(= 53.1379 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g}\)

stem:
Find the formula mass of

i. \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)

ii. \(\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2}\)
solution:
i. Formula mass of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)

= average atomic mass of Na + average atomic mass of Cl

\(= 23.0\ \mathrm{u} + 35.5\ \mathrm{u} = 58.5\ \mathrm{u}\)

ii. Formula mass of \(\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2}\)

= average atomic mass of Cu + 2 × (average atomic mass of nitrogen + average atomic mass of three oxygen)

\(= (63.5) + 2(14 + 3 \times 16) = 187.5\ \mathrm{u}\)
_note: p-07 right column. ⚠ THIS IS THE PROBLEM/SOLUTION GAP: the book prints NO `Solution :` label for 1.4 — the working begins directly with `i. Formula mass of NaCl = ...`. Verified on the rendered page. All six other worked examples carry the label.

stem: Calculate the number of moles and molecules of urea present in 5.6 g of urea.
solution:
Mass of urea \(= 5.6\ \mathrm{g}\)

Molecular mass of urea, \(\mathrm{NH_2CONH_2}\)

= 2 (average atomic mass of N) + 4 (average atomic mass of H) + 1 (average atomic mass of C) + 1 (average atomic mass of O)

\(= 2 \times 14\ \mathrm{u} + 1 \times 12\ \mathrm{u} + 4 \times 1\ \mathrm{u} + 1 \times 16\ \mathrm{u} = 60\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(\therefore\) molar mass of urea \(= 60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Number of moles \(= \dfrac{\text{mass of urea in g}}{\text{molar mass of urea in g mol}^{-1}} = \dfrac{5.6\ \mathrm{g}}{60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.0933\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Number of molecules = Number of moles × Avogadro's constant

Number of molecules of urea

\(= 0.0933 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{molecules/mol}\)

\(= 0.5618 \times 10^{23}\) molecules

\(= 5.618 \times 10^{22}\) molecules

**Ans :** Number of moles \(= 0.0933\ \mathrm{mol}\); Number of molecules of urea \(= 5.618 \times 10^{22}\) molecules
_note: p-08 right column. ⚠ The `Ans : Number of moles = 0.0933 mol` on p-08 belongs to THIS worked example — it sits inside 1.5's own boxed region (the pink rule encloses it). It is NOT an exercise answer and is deliberately not counted in the keyed exercise total.

stem:
Calculate the number of atoms in each of the following

i. 52 moles of Argon (Ar)

ii. 52 u of Helium (He)

iii. 52 g of Helium (He)
solution:
i. 52 moles of Argon

1 mole Argon atoms \(= 6.022 \times 10^{23}\) atoms of Ar

\(\therefore\) 52 moles of Ar \(= 52\ \text{moles} \times \dfrac{6.022 \times 10^{23}}{1\ \mathrm{mol}}\ \text{atoms}\)

\(= 313.144 \times 10^{23}\) atoms of Argon

ii. 52 u of Helium

Atomic mass of He = mass of 1 atom of He \(= 4.0\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(\therefore 4.0\ \mathrm{u} = 1\) He \(\therefore 52\ \mathrm{u} = ?\)

\(= 52\ \mathrm{u} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{atom}}{4.0\ \mathrm{u}} = 13\) atoms of He

iii. 52 g of He

Mass of 1 mole of He \(= 4.0\ \mathrm{g}\)

Number of moles of He \(= \dfrac{\text{mass of He}}{\text{mass of 1 mole of He}} = \dfrac{52\ \mathrm{g}}{4.0\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 13\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Number of atoms of He = Number of moles \(\times\ 6.022 \times 10^{23}\)

\(= 13\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{atoms/mol}\)

\(= 78.286 \times 10^{23}\) atoms of He.

stem: Calculate the number of moles and molecules of ammonia \((\mathrm{NH_3})\) gas in a volume 67.2 \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) of it measured at STP.
solution:
Volume of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) at STP \(= 67.2\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)

molar volume of a gas \(= 22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}\)

Number of moles (n) \(= \dfrac{\text{Volume of the gas at STP}}{\text{Molar volume of gas}}\)

Number of moles of \(\mathrm{NH_3} = \dfrac{67.2\ \mathrm{dm^3}}{22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}} = 3.0\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Number of molecules = Number of moles \(\times\ 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{molecules mol}^{-1}\)

Number of molecules of \(\mathrm{NH_3} = 3.0\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{molecules mol}^{-1}\)

\(= 18.066 \times 10^{23}\) molecules
